hints: Focus on what the word elimination tells you, atoms are removed from the molecule to form a new bond.
Bromoethane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, and elimination removes $\text{HBr}$ from adjacent carbons.
Think about what is left when you lose H and Br from two carbons, and what type of bond must form to complete the valency.
walkthrough:
**Remember what elimination does**

Great start. Substitution swaps Br for another group, but elimination removes Br plus a H from the next carbon.

That loss creates a carbon-carbon double bond, so a haloalkane becomes an alkene.

**Apply it to bromoethane**

Bromoethane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. With hot ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$, we remove $\text{HBr}$.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH (ethanolic, heat)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Name the product**

$\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ with two carbons and a double bond is ethene.

That is the only elimination product here, the others all come from substitution reactions.

options.A: Ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, is made by substitution (hydrolysis) with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, where OH replaces Br. It is not an elimination product because no double bond is formed.
options.B: Ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, is correct. Hot ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ removes $\text{HBr}$ from bromoethane to form the C=C double bond. This is the classic dehydrohalogenation elimination.
options.C: Ethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, is made by nucleophilic substitution with excess hot ammonia, where $\text{NH}_2$ replaces Br. No small molecule is eliminated and no double bond forms.
options.D: Propanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, is made by substitution with $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol, where CN replaces Br and adds a carbon. This is chain extension by substitution, not elimination.
